lead: Every survey, every quality check and every A/B test on a shopping app starts with a small set of observed values. That set is a sample. The full collection it comes from is the population. A number computed from the sample, such as the mean, is a statistic. Because the sample is chosen at random, the statistic changes from sample to sample. Its probability distribution is called a sampling distribution. This chapter sets up these words carefully, because estimation in the rest of Unit 5 depends on them.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 data summaries and Unit 2 probability basics.

blocks.text: A population is the complete set of units under study. Its size is N. The units can be people, UPI transactions, bulbs from a factory, or cricket scores. A sample is a subset of n units selected from the population. N is the population size and n is the sample size; both are counts, so N = 4 and n = 2 are possible small values in a textbook example.

A parameter is a fixed number that describes the population. The population mean is μ, the population variance is σ², and a population proportion is p. These symbols are fixed for a given population, even if we do not know their values.
A statistic is a function of the sample values only. It may use x₁, x₂, …, xₙ and n. It may not use μ, σ², p, or any other unknown parameter. The sample mean is a statistic:

blocks.where: x̄ (read x-bar) is the sample mean; n is the number of observations; x<sub>i</sub> is the i-th sample value.

blocks.text: The sample variance S², the sample range, and the largest sample value are also statistics. A statistic is random before the sample is drawn and fixed after it is drawn. Some syllabi call it a sample statistic.

sections.h3: Random sampling and the sampling distribution

blocks.text: Random sampling is a rule for choosing units without favouring any of them. In simple random sampling without replacement, every subset of n distinct units from the N population units has the same chance. There are C(N, n) such subsets, where C(N, n) is the number of ways to choose n units from N. Each subset has probability 1/C(N, n). In simple random sampling with replacement, we draw n times and allow repeats; each ordered sample has probability 1/N^n.

The rule matters because it controls the statistic. Draw a different sample and x̄ changes. Over all repeated samples, x̄ has a probability distribution. That distribution is the sampling distribution of x̄. It lists the possible values of the statistic and their probabilities, or gives their density for a continuous statistic.

For example, take the population 2, 4, 6, 8 with N = 4. Samples of size n = 2 without replacement give six subsets: (2,4), (2,6), (2,8), (4,6), (4,8), (6,8). Each has probability 1/6. Their sample means are 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7. So the sampling distribution puts probability 1/6 on 3, 1/6 on 4, 2/6 on 5, 1/6 on 6, and 1/6 on 7. The mean of this distribution is 5, which equals the population mean μ. The general theory of the sample mean and variance is in 5.2.
A statistic used to estimate a parameter is called an estimator. The particular value from one sample is an estimate. Estimators are judged in 5.4.

sections.h3: Standard error, sampling error and non-sampling error

blocks.text: The standard error of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. It is written SE. For the sample mean, SE(x̄) measures the typical distance between x̄ and its own mean μ. When sampling is with replacement, or the population is infinite, SE(x̄) = σ/√n. When sampling is without replacement from a finite population of size N, multiply by the finite population correction √((N−n)/(N−1)).

blocks.where: σ is the population standard deviation; n is the sample size; N is the population size; SE(x̄) is the standard error of the sample mean.

blocks.text: The correction is close to 1 when n is small compared with N. It becomes 0 when n = N, because a census has no sampling error. These formulas use σ, so a statistician must estimate σ in practice; that step belongs to 5.4.

Sampling error is the difference between a statistic and the parameter that comes from looking at only part of the population. It is random and usually shrinks as n grows. Non-sampling error comes from a wrong sampling frame, non-response, a faulty measuring instrument, a data-entry mistake, or a biased question. A larger sample does not remove non-sampling error; it can even repeat the same bias more times. In a UPI transaction study, a missing set of small merchants is non-sampling error, while the gap between the sample mean and μ is sampling error.

examples.question: Daily UPI transaction amounts, in hundreds of rupees, for four customers are 2, 4, 6 and 8. Treat these four values as the population. (a) Find μ and σ². (b) List every simple random sample of size n = 2 without replacement and compute x̄. (c) Form the sampling distribution of x̄ and verify its mean equals μ.
steps: The population size is N = 4. The population mean is μ = (2+4+6+8)/4 = 20/4 = 5 hundred rupees.
The population variance is σ² = [(2−5)²+(4−5)²+(6−5)²+(8−5)²]/4 = (9+1+1+9)/4 = 20/4 = 5 (hundred rupees)². The population standard deviation is σ = √5 ≈ 2.236 hundred rupees.
The number of samples without replacement is C(4,2) = 6.
Each of the six samples has probability 1/6, so P(x̄=3)=1/6, P(x̄=4)=1/6, P(x̄=5)=2/6, P(x̄=6)=1/6, P(x̄=7)=1/6.
The mean of the sampling distribution is (3+4+5+5+6+7)/6 = 30/6 = 5 hundred rupees, which equals μ.
examples.answer: The sampling distribution is P(x̄=3)=1/6, P(x̄=4)=1/6, P(x̄=5)=1/3, P(x̄=6)=1/6, P(x̄=7)=1/6, and its mean is 5 hundred rupees, equal to μ.
examples.check:
from itertools import combinations
pop = [2, 4, 6, 8]
N = len(pop)
mu = sum(pop)/N
sigma2 = sum((x-mu)**2 for x in pop)/N
print(mu)
print(sigma2)
means = []
for c in combinations(pop, 2):
    m = sum(c)/2
    means.append(m)
    print(m)
print(sum(means)/len(means))

traps: Treating μ as a statistic. μ is a fixed population parameter; x̄ is the statistic that changes from sample to sample.
Writing a statistic that contains an unknown parameter, such as (x̄−μ)/σ when μ and σ are unknown. A statistic must be computable from sample values alone.
Using 1/N^n for simple random sampling without replacement. Without replacement the probability of each subset of size n is 1/C(N,n), not 1/N^n.
Calling the sample standard deviation S the standard error. Standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic.
Confusing sampling error with a data-entry mistake. Sampling error comes from observing only part of the population; non-sampling error comes from frames, non-response, measurement or recording.

quiz.q: Define population, sample, parameter and statistic in one line each.
quiz.a: Population: all units under study, size N. Sample: selected units, size n. Parameter: a fixed population value such as μ. Statistic: a function of sample values only, such as x̄.

quiz.q: Why may a statistic not contain μ?
quiz.a: A statistic must be computable from the sample alone. If μ is unknown, any expression containing μ cannot be evaluated from the sample, so it is not a statistic.

quiz.q: State one difference between simple random sampling with replacement and without replacement.
quiz.a: With replacement, repeats are allowed and each ordered sample has probability 1/N^n. Without replacement, repeats are not allowed and each subset of size n has probability 1/C(N,n).

quiz.q: For the population 2, 4, 6, 8 and n = 2 without replacement, find the probability of the sample (4,8) and its sample mean.
quiz.a: There are C(4,2)=6 samples, so P(4,8)=1/6. The sample mean is x̄=(4+8)/2=6 hundred rupees.

quiz.q: A population has σ² = 5, N = 4 and a sample of size n = 2 is taken without replacement. Compute SE(x̄).
A larger sample reduces sampling error. Give a situation where a larger sample still gives a misleading estimate.
quiz.a: If the sampling frame leaves out small merchants from a UPI study, a larger sample of the same frame repeats the same bias. This is non-sampling error; increasing n does not remove it.

quiz.q: A student writes T=(x̄−μ)/(S/√n) and calls it a statistic. Is this correct when μ is unknown? Explain.
quiz.a: No. When μ is unknown, T contains μ and cannot be computed from the sample alone. If μ is known, T is a function of sample values and known constants, so it can be called a statistic.

beyond: Not for the exam. Sampling distributions are the engine behind A/B testing in product teams, control charts in manufacturing, and bootstrap confidence intervals in modern statistics. Survey organisations use finite population correction and design weights because real samples are rarely simple random samples. Search for 'bootstrap', 'finite population correction', 'sampling frame', and 'design effect' to go further.
